auth.reasonEditEntry: Proposing a change publishes your version alongside the existing one — nothing is overwritten and nothing is lost. Connect an account to propose it.
auth.reasonLanguage: Registering a language publishes a record under your name. Connect an account to add it.
auth.reasonSource: Describing a work publishes a record every citation of it will render from. Connect an account to describe it.
auth.reasonGrammar: A language's grammar is declared in a record you author. Connect an account to edit it.
auth.reasonTranslate: A translation is an assertion you publish and stand behind. Connect an account to add or correct one.
auth.reasonCognate: A cognate is an assertion you publish and stand behind. Connect an account to add one.

hero.title: The omnilingual dictionary
hero.subtitle: Leksis is a distributed, multilingual dictionary, with a low entry barrier for the world's under-resourced languages — built one richly described word at a time.

points.own: Own your contributions — every entry lives on your own AT Protocol server, never locked inside ours.
points.universal: Built for every language — designed from the ground up for low-resource and minority languages, not retrofitted from a big one. Unilike Wiktionary, we don't have to replicate dictionary for every language, the definitions are homolingual and translations helps learners fill the gaps.
points.depth: Structure over density — one richly annotated entry is worth more than a pile of raw text. Through its complex design, the dictionary breaks the barriers between languages and between new learners and professional lexicographers. This design is thought to counter resource scarcity and to describe exhaustively the world's languages with minimum redundancy.

relationEditor.title: Relate “{{word}}” to another word
relationEditor.intro: The assertion will live as a record on your own PDS, pointing at both entries as they are now. It is symmetric — you are not adding a translation to one word, you are stating that two senses correspond.
relationEditor.reaffirmIntro: This relation is withheld because an entry has changed since it was written. Re-pick the senses it means today and publish it again to revive it.
relationEditor.equivalenceHelp: Translation and synonymy are the same assertion: a synonym is a translation whose two languages are equal. Only these are followed when chaining translations.
relationEditor.antonymHelp: Stored and shown on both words, but never followed when chaining translations — an opposite inverts meaning.
relationEditor.targetLanguageHelp: Pick the language it belongs to — the same language for a synonym or an opposite.
relationEditor.noWordFound: No entry with that spelling yet. It has to exist before it can be related to.
relationEditor.wholeEntryHelp: Every sense, including ones added later — the broadest claim, and the one that goes stale most easily.
relationEditor.notesHelp: Caveats about the assertion itself — a partial equivalence, a register it holds in. One per line. Kept on the record, not in the index.
relationEditor.deleteHint: Removes your own record from your PDS. If someone published an earlier version of this relation, that version becomes current again — withdrawing yours is not the same as removing the relation.
relationEditor.staleSideWarning: This address no longer matches any sense of the entry as it stands today — that is why the relation is withheld. Pick the senses it means now.
relationEditor.coarseHint_other: Claims all {{count}} senses — a broad assertion, and one that goes stale as soon as either entry gains a sense.

errors.sides: A relation needs exactly two sides.
errors.entry-uri: One side does not point at a record.
errors.language: One side's language tag is not well-formed.
errors.place: One side addresses senses that cannot exist.
errors.self: Both sides name the same senses of the same entry — that asserts nothing.
errors.notesUnreadable: This relation's own record could not be read, so editing it would discard any remarks it carries. Try again in a moment.

cognates.title: Cognates
cognates.hint: Words sharing a historical origin with this one. The chain of forms behind them is prose, told in the etymology; this is the part the dictionary can follow, so it reaches words nobody linked to this one directly.
cognates.empty: No cognate has been recorded for this word yet. If you know a word — in any language, including a historical or reconstructed one — that shares its origin, link the two.
cognates.distanceHint: Distance counts the assertions between two words. It says how the dictionary got there, not how closely the words are related.
cognates.truncated: This network is larger than can be shown at once — only part of it is displayed.
cognates.unresolvedSide: This word's entry is not indexed — the spelling comes from the cognate's own record.
cognates.addHint: Assert that this word and another share a historical origin.
cognates.parkedHint: These assertions cannot currently be vouched for, so they are kept out of the network until someone re-affirms them.
cognates.syncing: Publishing to the network — this cognate will appear here once indexed.

cognateEditor.title: Add a cognate of “{{word}}”
cognateEditor.intro: The assertion will live as a record on your own PDS, pointing at both entries. It is symmetric and says one thing: these two words share a historical origin. Which came first, and by what route, belongs in each entry’s etymology.
cognateEditor.reaffirmIntro: This cognate is withheld because one of its entries is no longer readable. Re-pick the word it means today and publish it again to revive it.
cognateEditor.targetLanguageHelp: Pick the language it belongs to. The same language is valid — two words of one language can descend from one origin by different routes.
cognateEditor.noWordFound: No entry with that spelling yet. It has to exist before it can be linked to — including a historical or reconstructed form, which is an entry in its own language like any other.
cognateEditor.notesHelp: A source, a caveat that the cognacy is disputed, or the mechanism if you know it. One per line. Kept on the record, not in the index.
cognateEditor.notesPlaceholder: Borrowed rather than inherited; see Matasović 2009.
cognateEditor.deleteHint: Removes your own record from your PDS. If someone published an earlier version of this cognate, that version becomes current again — withdrawing yours is not the same as removing the cognate.

errors.self: Both sides name the same entry — a word shares an origin with itself, which asserts nothing.

createEntry.title: Add “{{word}}” to {{language}}
createEntry.intro: The entry will live as a record on your own PDS; the network indexes it from there. Anyone can improve it later — records prove authorship, not ownership.
createEntry.orthographyHelp: All valid written forms — variants, archaic or regional spellings included.
createEntry.transcriptionHelp: Phonetic transcription in the International Phonetic Alphabet.
createEntry.duplicateWarning_one: {{count}} existing entry already uses this spelling in this language — check it isn't the same word before publishing.
createEntry.duplicateWarning_other: {{count}} existing entries already use this spelling in this language — check they aren't the same word before publishing.
createEntry.categoriesHelp: The word's grammatical categories, picked from what this language has declared. Each shows the name this language gives it.
createEntry.categoriesNoneBound: This language has not declared any grammatical vocabulary yet. Declare it from the language page, or write a tag below.
createEntry.categoryManualHelp: For a tag this language has not bound yet — a bot's, or one you are about to declare. It will show as written until someone gives it a name here.
createEntry.todoHelp: Tasks this version still needs — one per line, so several bots or editors can each track their own. Reviewers see them on the entry; an empty list marks the entry as complete.
createEntry.todoItemPlaceholder: e.g. verify the definitions against the source
createEntry.laterFields: Example sentences, recordings and dialectal forms join the entry in later milestones.
createEntry.introModify: Your proposal is published as a record on your own PDS and becomes the entry's current version. The previous version is archived, never lost.
createEntry.definitionsHelp: Written in the language itself. Arrange them with the arrows: ↑ ↓ move a definition through the list (crossing group edges), → nests it one level deeper, ← brings it back up — up to three levels, numbered like a dictionary (A. I. 1.). A heading with sub-senses carries its own notes but no text.
createEntry.definitionsInvalid: These definitions don't form a valid hierarchy yet — every deepest sense needs its own text.
createEntry.groupNotesHelp: A heading over the senses nested below — its notes apply to all of them (e.g. add the abbreviation “v.t.” / “transitive verb” once here instead of on every sense).
createEntry.plainNotePlaceholder: A remark that is neither a label nor definition text…
createEntry.otherFormsHelp: Other grammatical forms — plural, gerund, construct state… Each is a spelling plus the tags saying which form it is (drawn from the same pool as the categories). Inflected forms are searchable, so they lead back to this entry.
createEntry.notesLegendHelp: Free-text notes shown below the definitions — usage remarks, provenance, editorial comments.
createEntry.entryNotePlaceholder: A remark about the whole entry…
createEntry.referencesHelp: Sources for this entry, shown at the bottom. Each has a display text and, optionally, a link.

errors.writeFailed: The entry could not be written to your PDS. Try again.

createEntry.formTagManualLabel: Tag for this form, typed by hand
createEntry.etymologyHelp: Where the word comes from, in prose, written in this entry's own language — one paragraph per box. Dates, uncertainty and disagreement between sources belong here: a word's history rarely fits a form. To state that this word and another share an origin in a way the dictionary can follow, add a cognate on the entry's page instead.
createEntry.examplesHelp: Sentences showing this sense in use, written in the entry's own language. Each may name the work it was taken from — the citation a reader sees comes from that work's own record, so it is written once and stays correctable.
createEntry.exampleTextPlaceholder: A sentence using the word in this sense…
createEntry.exampleSourceSearchPlaceholder: Search the works described for this language…
createEntry.exampleSourceNoResults: No described work matches. Cite its OCLC number below, or describe it.
createEntry.exampleSourceUndescribed: nobody has described this number yet
createEntry.exampleSourceIndexing: described — waiting for the network to index it
createEntry.exampleOclcInvalid: This is not an OCLC number — digits, with or without a catalogue prefix.
createEntry.exampleOclcHelp: A work nobody has described yet can still be cited: the reference is to the number, so the citation resolves the day somebody describes the work.

sourceEditor.title: Describe a source
sourceEditor.intro: A source is a work an example sentence can be cited from. Describing it once here is what lets every entry that quotes it render the same citation — and lets a typo be fixed in one place instead of in everybody's entries.
sourceEditor.introEdit: Your version becomes this source's current description. The previous one is archived, never lost.
sourceEditor.categoryHint: Only published works for now. A recording, a web page and a named informant are sources too, and this field is here so they can be added later without invalidating what has already been described.
sourceEditor.oclcHint: The number the work carries in library catalogues. It is this source's identity, which is what lets an example cite the work before anyone has described it. Prefixes and padding are fine — “(OCoLC)ocm00300375” is the same number as “300375”.
sourceEditor.oclcLocked: The number identifies this source, so it cannot be changed here. If it is wrong, describe the right one instead.
sourceEditor.lookupFound: Filled in from OpenLibrary — correct anything it got wrong.
sourceEditor.lookupNone: Nothing found for this number. Fill the fields in by hand: many of the works worth citing here were never catalogued.
sourceEditor.titlePlaceholder: The work's title as it is printed on it
sourceEditor.authorPlaceholder: Leave empty for an anonymous or collective work
sourceEditor.urlPlaceholder: https:// — a catalogue page or a digitized copy
sourceEditor.languagesHint: The languages the work covers. The entry editors of each will offer it, and each language's page will list it — so a bilingual dictionary belongs to both.
sourceEditor.mainLanguageHint: Set once, when the source is first described, and never changed afterwards: a citation that changed language under its readers would be a different work.
sourceEditor.mainLanguageLocked: Fixed for this source. If it is wrong, describe the work again under the right one.
sourceEditor.citationHint: What a reader sees after an example sentence taken from this work. Written here rather than in each entry, so correcting it corrects every entry that quotes it.
sourceEditor.longPlaceholder: The full bibliographic line the short form expands to.

errors.citation: Both citation forms are needed: the short one is shown after an example, the full one is what it expands to.

deleteRecords.oneIntro: It will be removed from your PDS. Nothing keeps a copy.
deleteRecords.allIntro: All {{count}} of your records will be removed from your PDS. This is as close to deleting your Leksis account as the protocol allows.
deleteRecords.notWithdrawal: This is not the same as withdrawing an entry. Withdrawing leaves a version explaining why, which others can read and contest. Deleting removes your record entirely — there is nothing left to undo it with.
deleteRecords.consequenceEntry: Entries: your version leaves the dictionary. If someone published an earlier version, theirs becomes current again; if yours was the only one, the entry disappears.
deleteRecords.consequenceRelation: Translations: the assertion leaves the graph, so the words it linked stop being translations of each other.
deleteRecords.consequenceLanguage: Language records: this withdraws the language's names and its entire grammar declaration — the labels, features and tables every reader of that language sees, not just your own view of it. If someone else has described the language too, their version takes over; if yours was the only one, the language itself leaves Leksis, and its words are left in a language nothing names.
deleteRecords.profileKept: Your preferences record is kept, so your interface language and languages of interest survive. Nothing else does.

deleteEntry.title: Delete “{{word}}”
deleteEntry.intro: This publishes a new version marking the entry as withdrawn — the previous content is archived, never lost, and the entry stays reachable at its current address to contest the deletion later.
deleteEntry.duplicateLabel: This is a duplicate of another entry
deleteEntry.reasonHelp: Required — explain why this entry is being withdrawn.
deleteEntry.reasonPlaceholder: e.g. duplicate, not an attested word…
deleteEntry.legacyNote: Anyone who already links to this entry will still be able to open it and see this reason.

grammar.title: Grammar & labels
grammar.intro: Declare the grammatical vocabulary this language uses, and how it is named here. What you bind is what the entry editor will offer — anything left unbound simply never comes up.
grammar.recordUnavailable: This language's record could not be loaded, so it cannot be edited safely.
grammar.l4RootHint: How a word's forms are laid out: which axis runs down the table, which runs across, one table or several, and what a reader sees without asking. Axes say what varies; they cannot say what the table looks like.
grammar.l4NoAxes: No axis is declared yet, so there is nothing to lay out. Declare what a category's forms vary over under Axes first.
grammar.l4AddHint: Only categories whose forms vary over something can be laid out.
grammar.l4CategoryHint: Blocks are shown in this order. Several of them is how an irregular paradigm is expressed — one table per tense, plus a list for the forms no grid reaches.
grammar.l4SummaryToggle: Show this block beside the headword
grammar.l4SummaryHint: A dictionary prints "rosa, rosae" and leaves the rest to the reader. Mark nothing and every block is shown.
grammar.l4RemoveLast: Removing the last block withdraws the layout, and forms fall back to a flat list.
grammar.l4DimensionHint: The first axis is the outermost: the ones after it nest inside it, and that nesting is what makes a header span several lines.
grammar.l4NoDimensions: Put at least one axis on a dimension — a table with none has no cells.
grammar.l4FixedHint: Pin an axis to one value and this block is that slice of the paradigm — the present indicative, say. The pinned value names the block and is part of every cell's address.
grammar.l4CellHint: Each cell shows the form's identifier. Click one to say this language has no such form; click it again to put it back.
grammar.l4TooLarge: These axes multiply out to more cells than a table can show. Split the block, or pin an axis to one value.
grammar.l4ItemHint: Pick one value per axis. A list is for the forms a grid does not reach — an infinitive, a supine — and for the short run of forms printed next to the headword.
grammar.classesHint: A declension, a conjugation group, a mutation class — the sets this language sorts its words into. Universal Dependencies has no term for these, so nothing here is suggested: name the class, then name the classes a word can belong to. They are ordinary features, so they appear under Features too.
grammar.addClassHint: A capitalised name for the class as a whole, e.g. Declension, Conjugation — its members are named inside it.
grammar.lexicalHint: Register, domain and editorial usage — “archaic”, “familiar”, “neologism”, “by extension”. Group them the way this dictionary uses them: name the group, then name the labels inside it. They are picked on an entry or a sense like any other label, but they never take part in the grammar: a word is not inflected for “by extension”, so these never become a category’s inherent feature, an axis of its forms, or a column of a table.
grammar.addLexicalHint: A capitalised name for the group as a whole, e.g. Register, Domain, Usage — the labels themselves are named inside it.
grammar.lexicalValuesHint: The labels of {{feature}} — “archaic”, “familiar”, and so on. Each is yours to name: Universal Dependencies documents no values for a feature it does not define.
grammar.abbreviationsHint: The plain abbreviations a dictionary spells out in its front matter — “udb.” for “un dra bennak”, “s.o.” for “someone”. They stand for no grammatical tag, so there is nothing to bind them to: the short form is what identifies them.
grammar.addAbbreviationHint: The abbreviated form, exactly as it is printed. Two abbreviations cannot share one.
grammar.classValuesHint: The classes a word can belong to under {{feature}} — a first declension, a second, and so on. Each is yours to name: Universal Dependencies documents no values for a feature it does not define.
grammar.posHint: The parts of speech a headword can take. The list is fixed, so the task visibly ends — add one below only if none of them fits this language.
grammar.featuresHint: Grammatical features this language uses, such as gender, case or tense. Bind a feature's name first; its values open up once you have.
grammar.valuesHint: The values {{feature}} can take in this language. Leave a value unbound and it never appears as an option anywhere.
grammar.usageCount_one: 1 indexed entry carries this tag — on the word, one of its senses, or one of its forms
grammar.usageCount_other: {{count}} indexed entries carry this tag — on the word, one of their senses, or one of their forms
grammar.usageSample: Show an entry that carries it
grammar.homolingualHint: Write it in this language, for a reader of this language — the way it would appear in a dictionary printed here.
grammar.noteHint: What this covers in this language, and where its border with a neighbouring one falls — the sentence a dictionary's front matter puts under the heading. Also in this language, and shown to readers beside the label.
grammar.notePlaceholder: e.g. the singulative: one item drawn from a collective, distinct from the plural.
grammar.mintLabel: Nothing in Universal Dependencies fits — {{tag}} declares this itself
grammar.mintHint: Check this only after looking for an existing term. Declaring your own is expected and legitimate, and it stays compatible as long as you say where it comes from.
grammar.udLoading: Looking up what Universal Dependencies documents…
grammar.mintPosHint: Capitals and digits, starting with a letter. Only for a part of speech none of the above covers.
grammar.addFeatureHint: A capitalised name, e.g. Gender, Case, Tense. A possessor's feature is written Number[psor].
grammar.addValueHint: Capitalised, or starting with a digit — e.g. Fem, Plur, 1.
grammar.unbindBlocked: Unbind its values first — they would otherwise be left pointing at a name nobody declared.

errors.defects: This cannot be published yet — a record whose declarations contradict each other is not indexed, so the version would be dropped without a word. Fix these first:
errors.stale: Someone published a new version of this record while you were editing. Reopen this dialog to start from theirs — publishing now would silently drop their changes.
errors.writeFailed: The record could not be written to your PDS. Nothing was changed.

issue.duplicate: {{key}} — bound twice, so which label applies is undefined
issue.unbound-atom: {{key}} — built on “{{atom}}”, which this language has not bound
issue.ungrounded-combination: {{key}} — no feature is declared inherent to the category it refines, so nothing leads to it
issue.single-item-binding: {{key}} — a single tag, which belongs with the parts of speech or the values
issue.inherent-axis-conflict: {{key}} — “{{feature}}” is declared both inherent to this category and an axis of it, so it is at once what the word is and what varies across its forms
issue.empty-axis: {{key}} — “{{feature}}” is declared as varying, but no values say what it varies over
issue.layout-unknown-axis: {{key}} — this table is laid out along “{{feature}}”, which is not declared as varying across this category's forms
issue.layout-repeated-axis: {{key}} — “{{feature}}” is on two dimensions of one table, so a single cell would need two of its values at once
issue.layout-foreign-coordinate: {{key}} — leaves out “{{atom}}”, which is not a coordinate of this table, so nothing is left out
issue.empty-layout-block: {{key}} — a block with nothing in it: no axis to lay out, and no form to print
issue.layout-too-large: {{key}} — its axes multiply out to more cells than a table can show, so it is not drawn at all
issue.lexicographic-in-grammar: {{key}} — uses “{{feature}}”, a lexicographic label set: it says how a word is used, not what it is or how its forms vary, so no paradigm can be built on it
issue.duplicate-abbreviation: {{key}} — two abbreviations share this short form, which is what identifies them

grammar.l2RootHint: Pick a category, then declare which features are part of what it is — its gender, its conjugation group — rather than something that varies across its forms. Named combinations appear here too, so you can go one step deeper.
grammar.l2NoPos: Bind a part of speech under Primitives first — a category is made of what this language has declared.
grammar.l2CategoryHint: The features declared inherent here are what the entry editor offers next, one step at a time, after a contributor picks this category.
grammar.l2WithdrawBlocked: Named combinations stand on this declaration — remove their names first.
grammar.l2DeclareHint: Only bound features are offered; bind a feature under Primitives first.
grammar.l2FeatureHint: One combination per bound value of {{feature}} — {{bound}} of {{total}} named. Naming is optional: where your tradition prints one label (“nf.”), name the combination; where it prints two (“n. f.”), leave it and the parts render on their own.
grammar.l2NoValues: No value of {{feature}} is bound yet — bind them under Primitives first.
grammar.l3RootHint: Pick a category, then declare which features vary across its forms — its number, its case, its tense — rather than being part of what it is. This is the other half of what you declared under Categories, and together they are the shape of the word's paradigm.
grammar.l3CategoryHint: The axes declared here are what the entry editor offers when labelling another form of a word, and what a later layer will lay out as a table. A feature already declared inherent to this category is not offered: a feature cannot both identify the word and vary across its forms.
grammar.l3DeclareHint: Only bound features are offered, minus those already inherent to this category. Bind a feature under Primitives first.
grammar.l3FeatureHint: Pick the values of {{feature}} that {{category}} actually varies over, and put them in the order they should be shown — that order is what a table's headers will print, and an identifier's alphabetical order is not a grammatical one.
grammar.l3PickSomething: Pick at least one value: an axis with none declares that something varies without saying what over, and cannot be published.
grammar.l3AddValueHint: Only values bound under Primitives are offered. A value this category does not use is simply left out — another category of the same language may range over a different set.
grammar.l5RootHint: Rules that generate a word's forms from its headword. Each table this language draws is a place rules can fill.
grammar.l5NoLayout: No table has been laid out yet. Rules fill the cells of a layout, so declare one first in the Layout tab.
grammar.l5UncoveredHint: These select a category this language has not laid out. They generate nothing until it does — open one to see what it addresses.
grammar.l5CategoryHint: Rules for this table. A narrower set — one declension, one conjugation — sits beside the general one and wins the cells it fills.
grammar.l5NoParadigms: No rules yet for this table.
grammar.l5AddHint: The category the rules apply to. It cannot be changed afterwards: it is what identifies the paradigm.

paradigmEditor.title: Inflection rules
paradigmEditor.intro: How this language builds a word's forms from its headword. Every entry of this category inherits them; an entry's own irregular forms always win their cell.
paradigmEditor.recordUnavailable: These rules could not be read from their author's server, so they cannot be rewritten here without discarding them. Try again shortly.
paradigmEditor.requiresHint: Principal parts the rules cannot derive — a genitive, a preterite. Write the message in this language: a contributor whose entry lacks the form reads it exactly as you write it.
paradigmEditor.requiresMessage: What to tell a contributor whose entry lacks this form
paradigmEditor.rulesOrderHint: The first rule whose condition the base satisfies fills the cell, so order matters. Put the specific ones above the general one.
paradigmEditor.rulesEmpty: No rules yet. Add a cell to fill.
paradigmEditor.ruleMatch: Only when the base ends in (pattern)
paradigmEditor.previewLemma: A headword to test the rules on
paradigmEditor.previewNothing: No rule matched this word yet.
paradigmEditor.previewMissingTitle: This word is missing a form the rules need

issue.empty-rules: A paradigm with no rules generates nothing — add at least one.
issue.unknown-base: This rule builds on a form nothing supplies: neither a required form nor another rule's target.
issue.base-cycle: These rules build on each other in a circle, so none of them can start.
issue.invalid-match: This condition is not a usable pattern.
issue.empty-message: A required form needs a message: it is what a contributor is shown when their entry lacks it.

errors.stale: Somebody else changed these rules while you had them open. Reload and make your changes again, so theirs are not overwritten.
errors.writeFailed: The rules could not be written to your PDS. Try again.
errors.loadFailed: These rules could not be loaded for editing. Try again shortly.
